item.title: Wednesday, July 1, 2026
item.description:
The vibe today

Today’s digest is dominated by a sense of “infrastructure exhaustion”—not in a negative sense, but in the realization that the next decade of discovery depends entirely on our ability to compute the “imcomputable.” Whether it is reaching NLO electroweak corrections for complex multi-leg vector-boson scattering (arXiv:2607.01174), or finally pushing lattice QCD into the regime of inclusive semi-leptonic decays (arXiv:2607.01116), the community is systematically narrowing the gap between theoretical prediction and experimental precision.

The mood is pragmatic and deeply technical. We are seeing a shift away from “discovery” as a singular, heroic event and toward a vision of physics as a high-precision, AI-augmented, and algorithmically optimized stack. Even the “new” physics papers today, like those targeting dark sector self-scattering or axion-superradiance, are built on the back of rigorous, multi-loop matching frameworks and lattice-calibrated non-perturbative methods. It is an era of tool-builders, and the tools they are forging are increasingly sophisticated.

Themes

Higher-Order Precision Tools

The push for sub-percent precision is no longer an aspiration; it is the current standard. Denner et al. arXiv:2607.01174 set a new bar for the LHC by providing the first NLO electroweak corrections for doubly-polarized ZZ scattering. This isn’t just a technical exercise; by isolating polarization states at the amplitude level, they provide the sensitivity required for high-luminosity LHC runs to distinguish subtle BSM effects from standard gauge-sector dynamics. Complementing this, Beneke et al. arXiv:2607.01413 tackle the power-suppressed region (Q²/E²) of QCD currents, resolving endpoint singularities in a way that finally makes multi-loop event-shape calculations tractable at higher orders.

Small-x Gluon Dynamics

The EIC era is effectively already here in the theoretical domain. Wang (arXiv:2607.00439) makes a significant move, proving that the gluon D-term—crucial for spatial tomography—cannot be extracted from simple leading-eikonal saturation models. By demonstrating that the D-term is fundamentally a sub-eikonal stress probe, Wang moves the field toward a more sophisticated, “stress-decorated” understanding of the gluon field that matches the precision demands of next-gen collider physics.

Quantum Information Lenses

Quantum information theory continues to bleed into conventional phenomenology. Pan et al. arXiv:2607.00971 propose using the tracker material itself as a polarimeter to probe the quantum entanglement of diphoton systems. While the significance at the HL-LHC is modest, the methodology represents a creative pivot: using experimental constraints—often seen as sources of noise—as active instruments to perform foundational tests of quantum mechanics at the high-energy frontier.

Lattice Renormalization Schemes

The lattice community is moving toward more robust, non-perturbative renormalization strategies. Black et al. arXiv:2607.00493 propose Gradient Flow (GF) schemes that bypass the cumbersome “backward-flow” constructions, allowing for a cleaner path to MS matching. This is paired with De Santis et al. arXiv:2607.01116, who demonstrate a concrete application of lattice methods to inclusive B_s decays—showing that lattice data can be reliably extrapolated to match OPE results, a vital step for testing the flavor sector.

Worth a look

  • arXiv:2607.01174 The cleanest of them all: NLO electroweak corrections to vector-boson scattering into doubly polarised ZZ pairs at the LHC — Denner et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: A masterclass in multi-leg precision, providing the necessary theoretical control for polarization-sensitive scattering observables at the HL-LHC.
  • arXiv:2607.00439 Sub-eikonal stress and model dependence of the small-x gluon D-term — Wang (hep-ph)
    • Why: A theoretically astute “no-go” result that forces a more rigorous approach to EIC-era spatial tomography and gluon distribution evolution.
  • arXiv:2607.01116 Inclusive B̅_s↦X_s̅c ℓν̅ decays from lattice QCD — De Santis et al. (hep-lat)
    • Why: Demonstrates that inclusive B-decays are finally accessible via first-principles lattice calculations, potentially resolving long-standing tension in the flavor sector.
  • arXiv:2607.00971 Quantum entanglement of photon pairs at proton-proton colliders — Pan et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: An original proposal to leverage tracker material as a polarimeter for fundamental quantum tests, shifting the role of detector materials from passive barriers to active analytical tools.

From the community

  • arXiv:2607.01496 Towards triggerless four-dimensional detectors for High Energy Physics collider experiments — Gligorov (physics.ins-det)
    • Why: A insightful look at the transition to 4D, picosecond-timing-capable detectors, exploring how this paradigm shift might render the traditional “trigger” architecture of collider experiments obsolete in the future.

Also noted

  • arXiv:2607.01317 No Evidence for Superradiant Axions in LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA GWTC-5 Binary Black Hole Spins — Ning et al. (hep-ph) — A massive hierarchical Bayesian analysis that significantly tightens the constraints on ultralight axions using 257 BH mergers.
  • arXiv:2607.01339 Electron stability constrains neutrino time delays — Bustamante et al. (hep-ph) — A clever proof that any LIV leading to neutrino time delays must also account for electron instability, largely killing the simplest LIV-based interpretations of neutrino speed anomalies.
  • arXiv:2607.01354 Local Conformal Predictions for Calibrated Surrogates — Dubey et al. (hep-ph) — An essential paper for the “ML-in-HEP” crowd, providing a way to make neural-network-based amplitude surrogates actually trustworthy via local calibration.

Deep dives

arXiv:2607.01174 — The cleanest of them all: NLO electroweak corrections to vector-boson scattering into doubly polarised ZZ pairs at the LHC (Ansgar Denner et al.)

Denner et al. report the first NLO electroweak (EW) corrections to the fully leptonic ZZ vector-boson scattering (VBS) channel. Using the double-pole approximation to preserve gauge invariance, the authors separate polarization states at the amplitude level and include factorisable EW corrections to both production and decay. They demonstrate that these corrections are substantial, reducing integrated cross sections by approximately 18% (–14% for longitudinal-longitudinal pairs, –18% for transverse-transverse).

This work is critical for the High-Luminosity LHC era, where VBS observables are expected to test electroweak symmetry breaking with high precision. By providing NLO EW control over polarization-sensitive observables—specifically transverse-momentum and angular distributions—the authors enable experimentalists to move beyond simple unpolarized cross-section measurements. The analysis reveals that while EW corrections are significant, they are relatively flat in many angular observables, reinforcing the utility of polarization fractions as a BSM-sensitive probe. A notable caveat is that this precision currently applies to the four-lepton channel; given the low cross-section, meaningful differential measurement will require merging multiple decay channels to overcome statistical limitations.

arXiv:2607.00439 — Sub-eikonal stress and model dependence of the small-x gluon D-term (Lei Wang)

Wang demonstrates that the gluon D-term cannot be extracted from leading-eikonal saturation models (like the standard dipole S_x or saturation profiles Q_s). The headline finding is a “no-go” result: the D-term is fundamentally a sub-eikonal stress probe—projected by the symmetric-traceless transverse stress T_g^ij—and therefore cannot be determined by the leading-eikonal momentum form factor A_g(t).

This provides a necessary theoretical correction for the EIC era, effectively de-coupling spatial tomography from simple eikonal assumptions. By constructing a gauge-invariant “stress-decorated” Wilson line operator, the paper establishes that the sign and magnitude of the gluon D-term depend on sub-eikonal target fields (e.g., F^i-). While the authors show that a specific “anti-aligned” response model leads to a stable negative forward D-term, the broader conclusion is that the D-term’s model dependence is a feature, not a bug, of higher-order gluon dynamics. The reliance on this specific response model remains a theoretical assumption, highlighting that current saturation models remain incomplete for full 3D gluon imaging.

arXiv:2607.01116 — Inclusive B̅_s ↦X_s̅c ℓν̅ decays from lattice QCD: computational strategy and a first physical result (Alessandro De Santis et al.)

De Santis et al. introduce a first-principles lattice QCD framework to calculate the inclusive decay rate of B̅_s →X_s̅c ℓν̅. The methodology bridges the gap between lattice data (computed at unphysical, lighter heavy-meson masses up to 4.3 GeV) and the Operator Product Expansion (OPE), which is valid in the heavy-quark limit. By employing a new technique for four-point correlator computation, they achieve a 7% total error on the inclusive decay rate using n_f=2+1+1 ETMC ensembles.

This result is a milestone for flavor physics, as it brings inclusive B-decays into the domain of non-perturbative lattice calculations, offering a path to resolve long-standing tensions in the flavor sector that have previously relied heavily on phenomenological inputs. The 7% error is dominated by the limited size of the current configuration set, though the methodology is explicitly designed for systematic reduction as larger datasets become available. The primary caveat is the extrapolation to the physical heavy-quark mass limit, which relies on the OPE remaining robust in the region where lattice data can currently be reliably produced.

item.title: Tuesday, June 30, 2026
item.description:
The vibe today

Today’s postings reflect a community that is rapidly modernizing its entire workflow, from deep theory calculations to the day-to-day coding pipeline. The overarching mood is one of rigorous preparation and infrastructure-building. Whether it is calculating cross-sections to unprecedented N³LO precision, rewriting old phenomenological engines to be navigated by LLM-based AI agents, or using quantum information metrics to resolve long-standing experimental tensions, the field is laying down the technical foundations required for the next decade of discovery.

There is also a palpable sense of physical systems coming online. We see this in the first year of on-sky data from the massive LSST Camera array at the Rubin Observatory, and in the sharp, highly coordinated theoretical papers mapping out the small-x gluon phase space in anticipation of the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC). Theorists are no longer just asking “what if” about new physics; they are building the high-precision machinery needed to extract it from the noise.

Themes

Light Higgsino Evasion Routes

The community continues to grapple with the tightening net around natural supersymmetry. In the last week, we saw how LZ direct-detection limits have severely cornered traditional light Higgsino dark matter (as detailed by Baer et al. in arXiv:2607.05648 and arXiv:2607.07921). Today, the search for a way out of this corner proceeds along two complementary fronts: future lepton colliders and specialized LHC topologies.

Hamaguchi et al. arXiv:2606.31013 provides a powerful counter-strategy to the LZ limits. They point out that while direct detection is highly sensitive when gauginos are light, its sensitivity collapses for heavier gauginos because Higgsino-gaugino mixing is suppressed. In this exact regime—where the Higgsino scattering cross-section drops deep below the neutrino fog—precision electroweak measurements of oblique parameters (M_W and sin²θ_eff) at future e⁺e⁻ colliders can step in, cleanly probing highly compressed Higgsinos up to 500 GeV. On the LHC side, Belyaev et al. arXiv:2607.00243 tackles the difficult compressed limit using a two-component scalar dark matter model (using a 3-Higgs Doublet Model framework), demonstrating that a dedicated search for soft opposite-sign dimuons accompanied by a hard jet can probe these elusive, compressed mass spectra.

Quantum Information as an Experimental Lens

Quantum information theory has transcended its role as a toy model framework and is now being deployed to solve practical, real-world issues in experimental data analysis.

A prime example is the work of Dixit et al. arXiv:2606.31996, which addresses the “fake” signals and degeneracies currently plaguing three-flavor neutrino analyses (a major theme in recent weeks, cf. arXiv:2607.06108). By mapping three-flavor neutrino oscillations to qubit-like representations, they show that the local minima of entanglement concurrence identify energy regions where the flavor state is closest to separability. Aligning the benchmark oscillation regions of NOνA and T2K with these minimum entanglement regions allows for a cleaner, joint parameter extraction that dramatically reduces the tension between the two experiments.

Meanwhile, the concept of “Magic”—a measure of how far a state is from being a easily-simulated stabilizer state—is popping up across the spectrum. Li et al. arXiv:2606.31501 shows that direction-averaged Magic in low-energy neutron-proton scattering is minimized at the CP-conserving point. This suggests a deep connection between fundamental symmetries and quantum computational complexity. In a similar vein, Alvarado et al. arXiv:2607.00229 tracks the production of magic states through electroweak Z bosons and dark photons, finding that Bhabha scattering is highly sensitive to electroweak effects on the underlying stabilizer state classes.

The Small-x Gluon Wigner Trilogy

In a remarkable single-author tour de force, Lei Wang has posted three papers arXiv:2606.31708, arXiv:2606.31712, arXiv:2606.31754 targeting the spatial and momentum distribution of gluons at small x. This represents a massive theoretical push to prepare for the spatial imaging capabilities of the EIC.

In arXiv:2606.31708, Wang proposes using azimuthal energy-flow moments in DIS dijet production to cleanly extract the elliptic gluon Wigner distribution without the soft-radiation leakage that plagues exclusive diffractive dijets. In arXiv:2606.31712, the author moves to the evolution of this distribution, demonstrating that the collinearly improved Balitsky-Kovchegov (IMST-BK) evolution alters the shape and node positions of the elliptic signal, rather than acting as a simple normalization shift. Finally, arXiv:2606.31754 constructs a normalized gluon Husimi phase-space distribution, showing that if you resolve it with a coarse-graining that adapts to the saturation scale Q_s(Y, b), the momentum distributions collapse onto a single scaling curve—revealing an emergent local scaling law in the high-density regime.

Next-Generation High-Energy Precision

The push to sub-percent precision at colliders is forcing theorists to compute terms that were once deemed impossibly complex.

Gehrmann-De Ridder et al. arXiv:2606.31286 presents the first fully differential calculation of boosted Higgs-strahlung (WH production) at N³LO in QCD. This is a monumental achievement: the N³LO corrections alter the boosted regime by +2%, lying entirely outside the scale variation bands of the previous NNLO calculation, while reducing the residual scale uncertainty to under 1%.

On the experimental tracking front, Lee et al. arXiv:2607.00087 achieves a major milestone by presenting the first complete, collinear-logarithmically matched calculations of jet substructure observables on tracks. By leveraging track-level tracking information rather than calorimeter clusters, this framework bypasses the spatial resolution limits of calorimetry, opening up a new regime of high-precision QCD measurements at the LHC.

Human-AI Co-Piloting in the Theory Stack

A quiet revolution is happening in how we build and execute our calculations. AI is moving from a tool for analyzing data to a co-developer of theoretical infrastructure.

Xiao et al. arXiv:2606.31214 introduces EasyScan_HEP 2, an upgrade designed specifically to be “agent-ready.” It exposes machine-readable command-line and config interfaces, allowing an LLM AI assistant to convert natural-language user requests directly into complex, multi-program parameter scan workflows.

On the calculation side, Kitazawa et al. arXiv:2606.31492 explicitly credits a human-AI collaboration for the development of high-order hopping-parameter expansion algorithms in lattice QCD. By utilizing a trie data structure designed in tandem with an AI coding agent, they successfully computed the daunting κ¹² term, demonstrating that AI can be a highly effective partner in pure mathematical physics.

Worth a look

  • arXiv:2606.31286 Boosted Higgs-strahlung off a W boson at next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order in QCD — Gehrmann-De Ridder et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: A milestone calculation for the Higgs precision program, showing that N³LO corrections in the boosted regime lie outside previous NNLO error bands and reduce residual scale uncertainty to sub-percent levels.
  • arXiv:2607.00087 Putting Jet Substructure on Track(s) — Lee et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: The first complete calculation of jet substructure observables on tracks up to four-point energy correlators at NLL, unlocking the exceptional angular resolution of tracking for precision QCD comparisons.
  • arXiv:2606.31175 Evidence for differential kinetic freeze-out of the ϕ(1020) meson in Pb-Pb collisions at √(s_NN) = 2.76 TeV — Neeraj et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: Excludes the bulk kinetic freeze-out point for the ϕ meson at 4.1σ, providing clean, quantitative evidence of a species-dependent freeze-out hierarchy driven by OZI-suppressed cross-sections.
  • arXiv:2606.31996 Quantum Information as a New Lens for Precision Neutrino Physics — Dixit et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: A highly original approach that uses quantum entanglement concurrence minima to find sweet spots that align NOνA and T2K data, successfully reducing the tension between the two datasets.

From the community

  • arXiv:2606.31806 The On-Sky Performance of the LSST Camera CCD Array — MacBride et al. (astro-ph.IM)
    • Why: A major milestone report detailing the first year of on-sky operations, readout optimizations, and troubleshooting (such as dealing with an electrical short) for the largest focal plane ever constructed (189 science CCDs) at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Also noted

  • arXiv:2606.31362 Running into tension: primordial black holes from ultra-slow-roll inflation, spectral running, and the Hubble tension — Sabogal et al. (astro-ph.CO)
    • Why: Shows that modifying the pre-recombination expansion history to resolve the Hubble tension (e.g., via Early Dark Energy) increases the CMB-inferred spectral running, which severely worsens the tension with ultra-slow-roll primordial black hole models.
  • arXiv:2606.31823 NNLO QCD predictions for tt̅W production at the LHC — Chen et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: Addresses the long-standing discrepancy where experimental tt̅W rates are consistently higher than SM predictions, evaluating the necessary two-loop amplitudes in the generalized leading-colour limit.
  • arXiv:2607.00096 Escape from Ostrogradsky via Hidden Ghost Parity — Bateman et al. (hep-th)
    • Why: Provides a rare and rigorous counterexample to Ostrogradsky’s “no-go” theorem for higher-derivative QFTs, utilizing a Krein space quantization and a hidden “ghost parity” to ensure positive probabilities.
